Tears wiped away
God will swallow up death and wipe away tears from all faces (also 7:17), combined with Isaiah 65:19, where weeping is heard no more.

Isaiah's promise (also 66:22) frames the final vision, while Isaiah 60:11,19-20 supply gates never shut and a city lit by God's glory (Revelation 21:23-25) and Isaiah 54:11-12 its jewelled foundations.
Jeremiah prophesied in Judah c. 627 to 586 BC, through Babylon's rise and the fall of Jerusalem.

Jeremiah warned Judah through the last decades of the monarchy that Babylon would destroy Jerusalem and the temple, and he lived through the siege of 587/586 BC. His book also contains oracles against the nations that climax in a long prophecy of Babylon's own fall (chapters 50 to 51).
Judgment on covenant unfaithfulness
Babylon's cup and Babylon's fall
The searcher of hearts
A new covenant

Revelation's portrait of Babylon the great in chapters 17 to 18 draws heavily on Jeremiah 50 to 51, combined with Isaiah and Ezekiel. From Jeremiah come the golden cup that makes the nations drunk, the city enthroned by many waters, the call for God's people to come out of her, and the sign-act of a stone thrown into the waters. Jeremiah also supplies the picture of God searching minds and hearts, and the bitter star Wormwood. Readers agree that Revelation uses Jeremiah's Babylon as a type; they differ on whether the antitype is first-century Jerusalem, imperial Rome, a future world power, or a recurring pattern of godless culture.
Golden cup that makes nations drunk
Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord's hand that made all the earth drunk; now the harlot herself holds the golden cup of her abominations, and the nations are drunk with the wine of her immorality.
Dwelling by many waters
Literal Babylon sat on the Euphrates and its canals; Revelation interprets the 'many waters' as peoples, multitudes, nations and languages (17:15).
The call to flee Babylon before its judgment (also Jeremiah 50:8 and Isaiah 48:20) is addressed to God's people, warning them not to share in her sins.
Repay her as she has done
Jeremiah's call to repay Babylon according to her deeds is intensified: 'pay her back double for her deeds'.
Stone thrown into the waters
Jeremiah's scroll tied to a stone and sunk in the Euphrates, with the words 'Thus shall Babylon sink', becomes a mighty angel hurling a great millstone into the sea.
Silence of the city
The sound of the millstones, the light of the lamp and the voices of bride and bridegroom fall silent in the ruined city, as Jeremiah threatened against Judah.
Burning mountain
Babylon is called a 'destroying mountain' to be made a burnt mountain; at the second trumpet something like a great burning mountain is thrown into the sea. The allusion is probable but not certain.
Wormwood
God threatens to feed his unfaithful people bitter wormwood (also 23:15); at the third trumpet a star called Wormwood makes the waters bitter.
Searcher of minds and hearts
The Lord who tests the heart and gives to each according to his ways (with Psalm 7:9) speaks to Thyatira as Christ.
To captivity, to the sword
Jeremiah's grim list of fates for unfaithful Judah is turned into a call for the endurance and faith of the saints under the beast.
Prophesied c. 593 to 571 BC among the Judean exiles in Babylon.

Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylon in 597 BC who received visions by the Chebar canal. He announced Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC, the glory of God leaving the temple, judgment on the nations, and then restoration: dry bones raised, Gog defeated and a new temple from which a river flows.
Glory of God on the throne-chariot
Eating the scroll
Judgment and the departure of the glory
Harlot city and lament over Tyre
New temple, river and city

Ezekiel shapes Revelation more structurally than any other book. Several scholars have observed that Revelation follows Ezekiel's broad order: throne vision, scroll, marking the faithful, scattering of fire on the city, the harlot, the lament over the trading city, resurrection, Gog and Magog, the birds' feast, and finally the measured temple-city with its river. John's own call (eating the scroll) mirrors Ezekiel's, and his final vision reworks Ezekiel 40 to 48. A key difference is that Ezekiel describes a temple, while Revelation's city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple; dispensational futurists usually expect Ezekiel's temple to be fulfilled separately in a millennial age, while many others see Revelation 21 to 22 as its fulfilment.
Throne with rainbow brightness
Ezekiel's figure on a sapphire throne surrounded by radiance like a rainbow is the model for John's throne vision, now with emerald and jasper, and with the Lamb soon at its centre.
Four living creatures
Ezekiel's creatures, each with four faces (human, lion, ox, eagle), become four creatures each with one of those faces, full of eyes and with six wings like Isaiah's seraphim.

Ezekiel eats a scroll written front and back that tastes like honey; John eats a little scroll, sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, and is told to prophesy again. The two-sided scroll also lies behind Revelation 5:1.
Mark on the forehead
A man with a writing case marks those who grieve over Jerusalem's sins before judgment begins; God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before the winds of judgment blow.
Coals scattered over the city
Burning coals from between the cherubim are scattered over Jerusalem; an angel throws fire from the altar onto the earth.
Merchants' lament and cargo list
Tyre's trading partners and goods, and the sailors' lament over the sunken city, shape the merchants' and mariners' lament over Babylon, whose cargo list ends with 'human souls'.

Ezekiel's Gog of the land of Magog, leading nations against restored Israel, becomes 'Gog and Magog', the nations from the four corners of the earth gathered after the thousand years. Interpreters differ on whether this is the same battle as Revelation 19 or a later one.
Birds' feast
The birds are summoned to eat the flesh of mighty men and horses on the mountains of Israel; an angel summons them to 'the great supper of God' after the rider's victory.
High mountain and measuring rod
Ezekiel is taken to a very high mountain where a man measures a temple; John is carried to a great high mountain where an angel measures a city. The same measuring motif lies behind Revelation 11:1.
River and trees of healing

The river flowing from the temple, with trees bearing fruit monthly and leaves for healing, flows instead from the throne of God and the Lamb, combined with Eden's tree of life. Ezekiel 48:31-34, the city's twelve gates named for Israel's tribes, also stands behind Revelation 21:12-13.
Set in the 6th century BC at the courts of Babylon and Persia; traditionally written by Daniel then, while many critical scholars date its final form to c. 167 to 164 BC under Antiochus IV.

Daniel tells of Judean exiles who stay faithful under pagan kings who demand worship, and records visions of a succession of empires pictured as beasts and as a great statue. These empires end when God gives the kingdom to 'one like a son of man' and to the holy ones.
Faithfulness under empire
Beasts from the sea
The Son of Man and the Ancient of Days
Time, times and half a time
Sealed and opened books
Resurrection and judgment

Daniel is one of Revelation's two or three most important sources, and G. K. Beale has argued that Daniel 2 and 7 provide a framework for whole sections of the book. From Daniel come the beasts from the sea, the Son of Man on the clouds, the white-haired Ancient of Days, the books opened at judgment, the time, times and half a time, and the angel swearing by him who lives forever. One notable change: what Daniel expects 'in the latter days' and must seal up, Revelation says 'must soon take place' and must not be sealed. Preterists, futurists, historicists and idealists read these links very differently, especially regarding which empire the fourth beast represents and whether the three and a half years are literal.
What must take place

Daniel's 'what will be in the latter days' becomes 'what must soon take place' (also 1:19, 4:1, 22:6). Many see this as signalling that Daniel's end-time kingdom has begun to arrive; how soon 'soon' is meant is a central debate between schools.
Beast from the sea

Daniel's four beasts (lion, bear, leopard and a ten-horned beast) are fused into one beast with ten horns that resembles a leopard, a bear and a lion. Many identify Daniel's fourth beast and Revelation's beast with Rome; futurists often add a final revived empire.
White hair like wool
Features of the Ancient of Days, hair white like wool and a throne of fire, are given to the risen Son of Man, joining divine and messianic imagery.
Coming with the clouds

The one like a son of man coming with the clouds (combined with Zechariah 12:10) is applied to Jesus (also 1:13 and 14:14). Preterists often link this to judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70; others to the second coming.
Books opened
Myriads of attendants stand before the throne (echoed in Revelation 5:11) and the court sits and books are opened; in Revelation the dead are judged from what is written in the books.
Mouth speaking great things
The little horn's boastful mouth becomes the beast's mouth uttering blasphemies, exercising authority forty-two months.
War on the saints

The horn makes war on the holy ones for 'a time, times and half a time'; the beast makes war on the saints, and the woman is protected for the same period (12:14). Futurists usually take it as three and a half literal years; others take it as symbolic of the church age or a limited time of trial.
Thrones and kingdom given to the saints

Judgment is given for the holy ones, who receive the kingdom; John sees thrones and those to whom judgment was committed reigning with Christ. The timing and nature of this reign is the core of the millennial debate.
Man clothed in linen
Daniel's heavenly figure with a golden belt, eyes like flaming torches, limbs like burnished bronze and a voice like a multitude shapes the portrait of the risen Christ.
Sealed and unsealed
Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end; John is told not to seal the prophecy, 'for the time is near'.
Oath by the one who lives forever
The man in linen raises his hands and swears by him who lives forever about 'a time, times and half a time'; the mighty angel raises his hand and swears that there will be no more delay.
Prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel c. 750 to 722 BC, before its fall to Assyria.

Hosea prophesied in Israel's last prosperous and chaotic decades, as kings were assassinated and Assyria loomed. His marriage to an unfaithful wife became a living parable of Israel's idolatry and of God's faithful, wooing love.
Covenant as marriage
Spiritual adultery
Wealth breeding pride
Wilderness as a place of renewal
'Not my people' becoming 'my people'

Hosea is a lighter source than the major prophets, but its marriage imagery helps shape Revelation's contrast between the harlot and the bride. The terrified cry for the mountains to fall on us comes directly from Hosea, and the self-satisfied boast of Laodicea echoes Ephraim's boast of wealth. The wilderness where God allures and nourishes his people stands behind the woman's refuge in Revelation 12. Some of these links are verbal and secure, others thematic, and commentators weigh them differently.
Mountains, fall on us

Israel's idolaters will say to the mountains 'Cover us' and to the hills 'Fall on us'; at the sixth seal people of every rank say the same to escape the wrath of the Lamb. Jesus also quotes the line in Luke 23:30.
'I am rich'
Ephraim boasts 'I am rich; I have found wealth for myself'; Laodicea says 'I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing', unaware of its poverty.
Refuge in the wilderness
God promises to allure his people into the wilderness and speak tenderly to them; the woman flees to a place prepared by God in the wilderness and is nourished there.
Betrothal and bride
God's promise to betroth Israel to himself in faithfulness becomes the marriage of the Lamb, whose bride is clothed in fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints.
My people, my God
'Not my people' will be called 'my people', and they will say 'You are my God'. The covenant formula reaches its fullness when God dwells with humanity and 'they will be his people'.
Date disputed: proposals range from the 9th century BC to after the exile (c. 400 BC); the setting is Judah and Jerusalem.

Joel responds to a devastating locust plague and drought, which he treats as a warning of the coming day of the Lord. He calls Judah to repentance, promises the outpouring of the Spirit, and foresees the nations gathered for judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat.
Locust army
The great and terrible day of the Lord
Darkened sun and blood moon
Harvest and winepress
Nations gathered for judgment
Waters from the Lord's house

Joel is a concentrated source for Revelation's judgment imagery. Its locust army, with lions' teeth and the sound of chariots, merges with the Egyptian locust plague in the fifth trumpet; its cosmic signs and question 'who can endure it?' shape the sixth seal; and its harvest and winepress become the double harvest of Revelation 14. The gathering of the nations to a valley of judgment is one background to Armageddon. Interpreters differ on whether these scenes describe events already fulfilled, still future, or recurring patterns of judgment.
Locusts like war horses
Joel's locusts look like horses, run like war horses and sound like chariots; Revelation's locusts are like horses prepared for battle with wings like the noise of many chariots.
Teeth of lions
The invading nation has the teeth of a lion; the locusts have teeth like lions' teeth.
Sun dark, moon blood
The sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the day of the Lord (also 2:10) appear at the sixth seal. Peter quotes the same passage at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).
Who can endure the day?
'The day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?' becomes 'the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?' (with Malachi 3:2).
Sickle, harvest and winepress

'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; the winepress is full' is split into two scenes: a grain harvest by one like a son of man, and a grape harvest trodden in the winepress of God's wrath. Some read the grain harvest as the gathering of the saved, others as judgment.
Nations gathered to the valley

God gathers the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat ('the Lord judges') for judgment; demonic spirits gather the kings to Armageddon. Whether Armageddon is a literal place of battle or a symbol is debated.
Prophesied c. 760 to 750 BC in the northern kingdom of Israel, though he came from Tekoa in Judah.

Amos, a herdsman and tender of sycamore figs, spoke during a prosperous era under Jeroboam II when the wealthy oppressed the poor. He warned that the day of the Lord would be darkness, not light, for a complacent Israel.
The lion has roared
God reveals his plans to the prophets
The Lord God of hosts
Day of the Lord as darkness
Justice for the poor

Amos is a minor but distinct source for Revelation, mainly for the theme of prophecy itself and for God's title. The angel's lion-like roar and the declaration that God's mystery was announced to his servants the prophets both echo Amos 3. Revelation's favourite title for God, 'the Lord God Almighty', matches how the Greek Old Testament often renders Amos's 'LORD God of hosts'. Several other links, such as darkness at noon, are thematic and shared with other prophets.
Revealed to his servants the prophets
The Lord does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets; the mystery of God will be fulfilled, 'just as he announced to his servants the prophets'.
The lion roars
'The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?' (also 1:2). The mighty angel calls out like a roaring lion, and seven thunders answer.
Lord God Almighty
The Greek translation of Amos frequently renders 'LORD God of hosts' as 'Lord God Almighty' (pantokrator). Revelation uses this title for God nine times, more than any other New Testament book.
Darkness at noon
God will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight; at the fourth trumpet a third of the sun, moon and stars is darkened. Exodus 10 is also in view.

Amos warns those who long for the day of the Lord that it will be darkness and inescapable, like fleeing a lion only to meet a bear. The sixth seal pictures the same inescapability, though this link is thematic.
Chapters 1 to 8 are dated 520 to 518 BC in Jerusalem after the return from exile; chapters 9 to 14 are undated and often placed later.

Zechariah encouraged the small, discouraged community that had returned from Babylon to rebuild the temple under Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua, while the Persian empire ruled. His night visions and later oracles promise God's presence, a humble king, a pierced one mourned by the nation, and the Lord's universal reign from Jerusalem.
Night visions of horses and riders
Lampstand and two olive trees
Measuring Jerusalem
The accuser rebuked
The pierced one
Living waters and endless day

Zechariah gives Revelation many of its most vivid images. The coloured horses become the four horsemen, the lampstand and two olive trees become the two witnesses, the seven eyes of the Lord become the Lamb's seven eyes, and the man with a measuring line becomes John measuring the temple and the angel measuring the city. Revelation's first prophecy of Christ's coming combines Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10, 'they will look on him whom they pierced'. Preterists tend to connect the mourning 'tribes of the land' with first-century Israel, futurists with a future national repentance, and idealists with all people at Christ's return.
Coloured horses
Zechariah's chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses patrolling the earth (also 1:8) become four horsemen released by the Lamb, now bringing conquest, war, famine and death.

Zechariah's single lampstand flanked by two olive trees, the two anointed ones (4:14, often seen as Joshua and Zerubbabel), become the two witnesses who are 'the two olive trees and the two lampstands'. Identifications of the witnesses vary from two individuals to the witnessing church.
Seven eyes
The seven eyes of the Lord that range through the whole earth belong to the Lamb, interpreted as the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.
Measuring line

A man with a measuring line goes to measure Jerusalem; John is told to measure the temple and its worshippers, and later an angel measures the holy city (21:15). Interpreters disagree on whether the temple is the literal temple or the church.
Satan the accuser
Satan stands at the angel's right hand to accuse the high priest and is rebuked; in Revelation the accuser of the brothers is thrown down from heaven.
Him whom they pierced
Those who pierced him look on him and mourn, combined with Daniel 7:13. John 19:37 cites the same verse using the same Greek verb, which differs from the standard Greek translation.
Endless day and living waters
A unique day without night and living waters flowing out from Jerusalem anticipate the city with no night and the river of the water of life.
No more curse
Jerusalem will dwell in security with 'never again a decree of utter destruction' (a ban or curse); in the new Jerusalem 'no longer will there be anything accursed'.
Usually dated c. 460 to 430 BC in Jerusalem under Persian rule, after the second temple was rebuilt.

Malachi addressed a disillusioned community whose priests offered blemished sacrifices and whose people doubted God's justice. He announced that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple, preceded by a messenger, Elijah, to refine and to judge.
The Lord's sudden coming
Who can endure his coming?
Elijah before the great day
Book of remembrance
God's name great among the nations

Malachi's influence on Revelation is modest and mostly thematic rather than verbal. It contributes the question of who can stand when the Lord appears, the expectation of an Elijah figure before the day of the Lord, which many see in the fire-breathing, sky-shutting two witnesses, and the image of a book kept before God. As the last book of the prophets in the Christian Old Testament, Malachi also shares with Revelation a closing emphasis on the coming of the Lord. Commentators vary in how many of these echoes they accept.
Who can stand?
'Who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears?' is echoed, with Joel 2:11, in the cry at the sixth seal.
Elijah before the day

The promised return of Elijah before the great day of the Lord is one background for the two witnesses, who like Elijah can shut the sky and call down fire (1 Kings 17:1; 2 Kings 1:10). Views range from a literal return of Elijah to a symbol of the church's prophetic witness.
A book of remembrance is written before the Lord of those who feared him; books are opened at the final judgment, and the book of life decides destinies. Daniel 7:10 and 12:1 are also in view.
God's name among the nations
From the rising to the setting of the sun God's name will be great among the nations, and incense offered; the song of the Lamb proclaims that all nations will come and worship.
The Olivet discourse (Matthew 24 to 25) is set in Jerusalem shortly before Jesus' death (c. AD 30 to 33); Matthew's Gospel is dated by scholars anywhere from the 50s to the 80s AD.

On the Mount of Olives, after predicting that the temple would be thrown down, Jesus answered his disciples' questions about when this would happen and the sign of his coming and the end of the age. The discourse draws on Daniel and the prophets and was spoken under Roman rule, about forty years before Jerusalem fell in AD 70.
Wars, famines and earthquakes
Great tribulation
False christs and false prophets
Cosmic signs and the Son of Man's coming
Gathering of the elect
Watchfulness: the thief in the night

Revelation does not quote Matthew, but many commentators note a close resemblance between the sequence of the seals in Revelation 6 and the signs Jesus lists in the Olivet discourse: war, strife, famine, death, persecution, then cosmic upheaval. Both draw on Daniel and Zechariah for the Son of Man coming on the clouds and the mourning of the tribes, and both warn of false prophets doing signs and of a coming like a thief. Whether the two describe the same events is central to the debate between schools: preterists link much of both to AD 70, futurists to a final tribulation, and others see a near fulfilment that foreshadows the end.
Wars, famine and pestilence
Wars and rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines and earthquakes parallel the first four seals; Luke 21:11 adds pestilences, matching the fourth rider.
Persecution and martyrdom
Jesus warns that disciples will be handed over and put to death; the fifth seal shows martyrs crying out, told to wait until their number is complete.
Sun darkened, stars fall
After the tribulation, the sun and moon are darkened and stars fall from heaven, drawing on Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4; the sixth seal uses the same images.
Tribes mourn as he comes on clouds

Both combine Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10: the Son of Man coming on the clouds and the tribes mourning. Whether 'tribes of the earth' or 'of the land' is meant is debated between preterist and futurist readers.
The great tribulation

Jesus speaks of great tribulation unequalled in history; the multitude in white are those 'coming out of the great tribulation'. Preterists usually place it in AD 66 to 70, futurists in a final seven-year period, and idealists across the church age.
False prophets with great signs
False christs and false prophets performing great signs to deceive the elect correspond to the second beast, later called the false prophet (19:20), who deceives by signs.
Four winds and a great trumpet
Angels gather the elect from the four winds with a loud trumpet; four angels hold back the four winds until God's servants are sealed, and the seventh trumpet announces the kingdom (11:15).
Coming like a thief
The householder who does not know when the thief is coming becomes Christ's warning 'Behold, I am coming like a thief' (also 3:3), with the blessing on the one who stays awake.
Traditionally written by the apostle John at Ephesus c. AD 85 to 95; some scholars propose an earlier date or a different author, and the relationship between the Gospel and Revelation is debated.

John's Gospel was written for believers in a setting of tension with the synagogue and the wider Greco-Roman world, possibly at Ephesus, one of Revelation's seven cities. It presents Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh, the Lamb of God and the fulfilment of Israel's feasts and temple.
The Lamb of God
The Word made flesh
God tabernacling with his people
Living water
'I am' sayings
Christ's victory over the world

The Gospel of John and Revelation share a remarkable set of images found almost nowhere else in the New Testament: Christ as the Lamb, as the Word of God, as the giver of living water, as the one 'pierced', and as the true temple where God dwells. Ancient tradition ascribes both to the apostle John, but from Dionysius of Alexandria in the 3rd century onward some have noted large differences in style, and many scholars today speak of a shared Johannine tradition rather than a single author. It is unclear whether either book drew on the other, so these links are best treated as shared themes. Revelation also uses the Gospel's language of 'conquering' and its emphatic 'I am' statements.
Lamb of God

John the Baptist names Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world; Revelation calls Christ 'the Lamb' twenty-eight times. The Greek words differ (amnos in the Gospel, arnion in Revelation).
The Word who was with God and was God reappears as the rider whose name is 'The Word of God'. Using 'the Word' as a title for Christ is characteristic of the Johannine writings.
God tabernacling
The Word 'dwelt' (literally 'tabernacled') among us; at the end 'the dwelling place (tabernacle) of God is with man', using the same Greek root. Revelation 7:15 uses it too.
Living water for the thirsty
'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink' (also 4:10-14) is matched by 'let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price' (also 7:17 and 21:6).
Both cite Zechariah 12:10 with the same Greek verb, which differs from the standard Greek Old Testament, a detail often noted as a link between the two books.
Light of the world
Jesus is the light of the world; in the new Jerusalem the glory of God gives light and its lamp is the Lamb.
Temple of his body
Jesus speaks of the temple of his body; John sees no temple in the city, 'for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb'.
Conquering the world
'I have overcome (conquered) the world' is echoed when Christ says he conquered and sat down with his Father; every letter to the churches ends with a promise to the one who conquers.
The shepherd
The good shepherd who lays down his life becomes the Lamb at the centre of the throne who will be their shepherd and guide them to springs of living water.
Paul's letters to the church at Thessalonica, written from Corinth c. AD 50 to 51 (Pauline authorship of 2 Thessalonians is disputed by some scholars).

Thessalonica was a Roman provincial capital in Macedonia where a young, mostly Gentile church faced persecution soon after Paul's departure. The letters answer questions about believers who had died and correct the idea that the day of the Lord had already come.
The Lord's descent with trumpet
The day of the Lord like a thief
The man of lawlessness
Deceiving signs and wonders
Christ's appearing in flaming fire

These letters are not sources Revelation draws on directly, but they share much of the same early Christian expectation and imagery. Paul's 'man of lawlessness', who exalts himself, sits in God's temple and works deceptive signs before being slain by the breath of the Lord's mouth, closely parallels Revelation's beasts and the rider's victory. Both use the trumpet, the thief in the night and Isaiah 11:4. The schools differ sharply on these parallels: futurists generally equate the man of lawlessness with a future antichrist matching the beast, preterists often place him in the first century, and some amillennial readers see a figure or power arising near the end of a long age.
Self-exalting enemy

The man of lawlessness opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god and takes his seat in God's temple; the beast utters blasphemies and is worshipped by all whose names are not written in the book of life.
His coming is by Satan's activity with false signs and wonders that deceive the perishing; the second beast performs great signs and deceives those who dwell on earth.
Slain by the breath of his mouth
Both draw on Isaiah 11:4: the Lord Jesus kills the lawless one with the breath of his mouth; the rider strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth, and the beast and false prophet are captured.
Revealed from heaven with angels
Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire to repay those who afflict his people; the rider, with eyes like flame, comes from heaven followed by heaven's armies.
The trumpet of God

The Lord descends with a cry, the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God (also 1 Corinthians 15:52); at the seventh trumpet the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord. Whether these trumpets mark the same moment is debated, especially in discussions of the rapture.
Like a thief in the night
The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, a saying traced to Jesus (Matthew 24:43); Revelation repeats it as Christ's own warning (also 3:3).
Written by an unnamed author to Jewish-Christian believers, most often dated in the 60s AD before the temple's destruction, though some date it later.

Hebrews addresses believers tempted under pressure and persecution to drift back from faith in Christ. It argues that Jesus is the great high priest who entered the true sanctuary in heaven, of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy and shadow.
